rights_basis: Letter dated 28 June 1863 (manuscript image header 'Carlisle Pa. June 28th 1863'; UNC item description), author Leonidas L. Polk d. 1892 (UNC page and Wikipedia infobox) -> public domain by date. (Civil War Day by Day, Louis Round Wilson Special Collections Library, UNC Chapel Hill; post by Biff Hollingsworth, 28 Jun 2013). Polk lists 2nd Lieutenant, 43rd North Carolina Infantry, Battle of Gettysburg (wounded there); OR vol. 27 pt 2 (Rodes's report, cached OCR) lists Daniel's (N.C.) brigade as 32nd, 43rd (Col. Thomas S. Kenan), 45th, 53rd NC and 2nd NC Bn, in Rodes's division. extraction_notes: HTML blog post (WordPress) with three manuscript page images plus an 'Item Transcription' block; ~7 KB of text, clean (no OCR). Segment by paragraph: header/dateline, army and route narrative, Carlisle conditions, closing and postscripts (about 6 passages). Keep the 'Item Description' and 'Item Citation' lines as the provenance record. Page images are at web.lib.unc.edu/civilwar/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/18630628000{1,2,3}.jpg.

Written 28 June 1863, before the battle: campaign context only, no Gettysburg fighting described.

written: 1863-06-27 (requisition issued at Carlisle by Maj. John A. Harman, Chief Quartermaster, 2nd Corps, ANV)
rights_basis: The underlying requisition is an 1863 Confederate Army manuscript (dated 27 June 1863 in the PDF transcription): public domain by date. But the only available copy is a Dickinson Archives item whose live page is gone; the archived item page carries 'Copyright (c) 2020 Archives & Special Collections at Dickinson College. All rights reserved.' and the archived PDF includes a modern dealer essay by Catherine Barnes (Historical Autographs) that is presumably her copyright. Quote only the 1863 requisition text, not the essay.
evidence: Entry URL http://archives.dickinson.edu/civil-war-resources/confederate-supply-requisition-authorities-carlisle -> 301 to https -> 404 'Page not found | Archives & Special Collections' (Drupal 11 site; its new navigation has no 'Civil War Resources' entry). Also 404: https://archives.dickinson.edu/civil-war-resources, /panel/civil-war-resources, /document-descriptions/<same slug>, and /sites/default/files/files_document|files_war/I-Friends-2013-5.pdf. Wayback availability API gave a 200 capture of the item page (2024-05-23): title 'Confederate Supply Requisition to "Authorities of Carlisle"', Date June 27, 1863, 6 pages, Location I-Friends-2013-5, Origin 'Gift of Friends of the Library', 'Transcript included'; text: 'Major John A. Harman, Chief Quartermaster with the Second Army Corps ... under the command of General Richard S. Ewell, issues a requisition to the "authorities of Carlisle Pa."'. I fetched the archived PDF (web.archive.org .../sites/all/files/files_war/I-Friends-2013-5.pdf, 6 pages, 2.7 MB): transcription reads 'Hd Qrs. 2d Army Corps A N V / June 27 1863 / To the authorities of Carlisle Pa. / By direction of Lt Genl R S Ewell. I require the following articles: 5000 Suits Clothing, including Boots, Shoes & Hats; 5000 Bushels Grain; 10,000 Pounds Sole Leather; 10,000 Pounds Horse Shoes; 400 Pounds Horse Shoe Nails; Also use of Printing Office & two Printers to report at once ... delivered at the Court House Square ... John A. Harman, Major & Chf QrMr, 2d Army Corps, ANVa'. The dealer essay says Ewell's 2nd Corps 'entered an undefended Carlisle ... remaining there until June 29'; OR vol. 27 pt 2 (cached OCR) independently says Ewell's corps 'occupied [Carlisle] on the 27th'. The accompanying 1864 letter ('Uncle Charlie' to 'Freddy' Vaux, dated June 20th 1864, Great Central Fair) matches the item-page provenance claim. Entry description 'demand for provisions served on Carlisle's civil authorities' is accurate in substance (it also demands clothing, leather, horseshoes and a printing office, so 'provisions' is loose).
extraction_notes: On the old site: item page + 6-page PDF (p1 modern cover sheet, pp2-3 page images of the manuscript and the provenance letter, p4-5 dealer essay with a line-by-line transcription of the requisition, p6 transcription of the 1864 letter). Text layer present on p1, p4-6 only; the manuscript itself is image-only. Segment: one passage for the requisition text (about 12 lines), one for the 1864 provenance letter; exclude the dealer essay from verbatim use. The live URL no longer resolves; the Wayback PDF for this item downloaded complete (2,685,477 bytes).
issues: Live link is dead (404) after the Dickinson Archives site migration; the whole /civil-war-resources/ section is gone from the new site.
Replacement exists only as Wayback Machine captures (item page 2024-05-23; PDF captured 2024-05-23). No live stable URL found.
Authenticity and 'not signed by Harman but written by an aide' are the dealer's (Catherine Barnes) own provenance research, not an archival finding.
Site-wide 'All rights reserved' notice on the Dickinson item page; dealer essay is third-party text.
Description says 'provisions'; the demand is for clothing, boots, leather, horseshoes and nails plus grain and a printing office.

written: 1863-06-21 (order date, Hdqrs. Army of Northern Virginia); broadside removed from a Carlisle tavern sign post on 1863-06-30
rights_basis: General Orders No. 72 is an 1863 Confederate Army order (public domain by date; the same order is printed in OR vol. 27 pt 3 p. 912, a US Government publication, so the quotable text should come from the OR entry at tier A1). The Dickinson item page says 'All rights reserved' (site-level notice); the 1 MiB-truncated archived PDF gave no usable text.
evidence: Entry URL http://archives.dickinson.edu/civil-war-resources/broadside-general-orders-no-72 -> 301 to https -> 404 (same Drupal 11 'Page not found' as 587). Wayback capture of the item page (2024-07-19) fetched: 'Broadside of "General Orders No. 72"', 3 pages, Date June 21, 1863, Location I-Original-1863-6, 'Broadsides and Posters', Event 'Invasion of Carlisle / Invasion of Pennsylvania'; text: 'These Confederate Army general orders, from General Robert E. Lee to Lieut. General Richard Ewell, are posted publicly in Carlisle ... "While in the enemy's country," the document warns that "the following regulations... will be strictly observed... and any violation of them promptly and rigorously punished."' and 'a handwritten note by Joseph A. Murray explains how he removed this broadside "from the sign post of Hannon's Tavern, Hanover street ... on Tuesday morning, June 30, 1863, as the Rebels, under Ewell, were leaving town"'. Independent check in cached OR vol. 27 part 3 OCR (historian-src/raw/or27/normalized-3.txt, read only): 'General Orders, No. 72. Hdqrs. Army of Northern Virginia, June 21, 1863. While in the enemy's country, the following regulations for procuring supplies will be strictly observed, and any violation of them promptly and rigorously punished. I. No private property shall be injured or destroyed by any person belonging to or connected with the army ...' and a cross-reference 'See General Orders, No. 72, p. 912'. The index line lists 'No. 72, 912'. Description claim 'Lee's order regulating the army's conduct toward private property, as posted in town' is accurate. The Wayback copy of the item PDF (I-Original-1863-6.pdf) was cut off at exactly 1,048,576 bytes (0 pages parsed, no text streams), so the broadside's image and any transcript could not be read.
extraction_notes: Do not ingest from Dickinson. The order text should be segmented from the OR vol. 27 pt 3 p. 912 entry (numbered paragraphs I-V seen in the OCR; further paragraphs follow). The broadside's own value is the provenance note by Joseph A. Murray (removed 30 June 1863), which is only on the dead Dickinson page and its Wayback capture.
issues: Live link dead (404); no live replacement found (new site does not carry the Civil War Resources section).

Title date range 'June 27-30, 1863' is the posting period, not the order date: the order is dated 21 June 1863 (Dickinson page and OR vol. 27 pt 3 p. 912). The start date 27 June is not on the item page.
Duplicates the content of OR vol. 27 pt 3 p. 912 already in the Official Records list; the broadside adds only the posting provenance.
Dickinson describes it as 'from Lee to Lieut. General Ewell'; it is a general order to the whole army.
Archived PDF truncated at 1 MiB: page images and any transcript unverified.

written: 1863-06-28 (dateline 'Camp in the Park of Dickinson College, Carlisle Penn.')
rights_basis: Letter dated 28 June 1863 (visible on the scan); a faithful scan of a 19th-century manuscript letter, public domain by date. The PDF was made by Cooper Wingert of the Dickinson House Divided Project (PDF metadata author, created 12 June 2018, 'Mac OS X Quartz PDFContext'); the House Divided pages show '(c) Content 2007-2010 by Dickinson College' and no license for the PDF. No transcription exists to quote. Repository ownership (Atlanta History Center) is stated only in the House Divided blog post.
evidence: Entry URL http://housedivided.dickinson.edu/sites/blogdivided/files/2018/06/Underwood-June-28-1-3.pdf -> 301 to https -> 200 application/pdf, 8,204,661 bytes, Last-Modified 12 Jun 2018; no robots.txt on the host (404). I rendered all 3 pages: p1 header 'Camp in the Park of Dickinson College, Carlisle Penn. June 28th 1863 / Messrs J.R.T. & M.L. Underwood / My Dear Little Brothers' (answering a letter received that morning; 'I left Fredericksburg'); p2 'I am now writing in a few feet of the old College ... Carlisle is a very beautiful City ... within 18 Miles of Harrisburg ... I have written 3 letters since I have been on the march; one while at Culpeper CH Va, one at Williamsport Md and another at Greencastle Pa'; p3 closes 'The love of your Brother W.J. Underwood'. An archive mark '77-535-09B' appears at the foot of p2 (no institution named). PDF has no text layer (3 pages, 0 chars, each page 3 images). The House Divided blog post 'Beyond Gettysburg: Primary Sources for the Gettysburg Campaign' (Cooper Wingert, 11 Jun 2018) labels the same link 'William J. Underwood Letter (4th Georgia) - camps on the Dickinson College campus (Atlanta History Center)'; the regiment and the Atlanta History Center claim are repeated from that post and are not stated in the scan. Context check: OR vol. 27 pt 2 (Rodes's report, cached OCR) shows the 4th Georgia in Doles's Georgia brigade of Rodes's division, the same division as Daniel's brigade that Polk's letter (586) places at Carlisle on 28 June, so '4th Georgia at Carlisle' is plausible but Underwood is not named in OR vol. 27. Description claim 'camped on the Dickinson College campus' is confirmed by the dateline; 'original at Atlanta History Center' is not independently confirmed.
extraction_notes: Image-only PDF, handwritten manuscript (p1-2 letter sheets, p3 a landscape scrap carrying the end of the letter and signature). No OCR or transcription available; to quote it a human transcription from the scan is needed. Segment by manuscript page if transcribed (3 passages). Use the https URL.
issues: Regiment '4th Georgia' and 'Atlanta History Center' are not shown anywhere in the PDF; they come from the House Divided post only (unverified).
Image-only: no free full text exists in machine-readable form; transcription would be our own derivative.
No license or rights statement on the PDF or hosting page; Dickinson footer claims content copyright 2007-2010.
Page 3 is a separate smaller sheet that continues mid-sentence ('...be with you to assist in getting the wheat'); order of pages assumed from the file.
Contemporary and campaign-period (Carlisle, 28 June); not a battle account.

This the greatest of all battles in modern times almost. It was terrific and destructive beyond description. I think our loss will not fall short of 20,000 killed and wounded...'; pp2-3 'I came here with Col Lightfoot and Major Culver of my regiment. They were wounded in the late memorable battle ... Natural passage segmentation if transcribed: (1) opening battle summary and casualty estimates, (2) travel to Staunton with the wounded Col. Lightfoot and Maj. Culver, Gettysburg first-day action and Ewell's march via Carlisle, (3) Carlisle, the 'Quakeress' and the conversation with Dr. Johnson, (4) leaving Gettysburg with the ambulance/wagon train and the South Mountain night attack. The HTML page is a JavaScript shell; use the stable item URL for citation and the dmwebservices API for metadata only.

rights_basis: Underlying diary is an 1863 manuscript by an anonymous writer (unpublished diary; anonymous works are public domain 120 years after creation, so well past). The transcription was made by Frank Kline per the House Divided post (not stated in the PDF), and the diary is held by the Cumberland County Historical Society (CCHS) per the post and the file name; any copyright in the transcription is unstated. House Divided pages show '(c) Content 2007-2010 by Dickinson College' with no license for the PDF. Tier A2 pending review of the transcription terms.
evidence: Entry URL http://housedivided.dickinson.edu/sites/blogdivided/files/2018/06/1863-Young-Girls-Pocket-Diary-CCHS.pdf -> 301 to https -> 200 application/pdf, 32,288 bytes, 2 pages, creator 'Word' ('Microsoft Word - 1863 Young Girl's Pocket Diary CCHS.docx', created 9 Aug 2018). pdftotext gave 4,130 characters with text layer. Text: daily entries from 'Wednesday, June 24, 1863' to 'Wednesday, July 8, 1863' (15 entries). Quoted claim checked: 'Monday, June 29, 1863: The Rebels are going in every house and stealing all they can the Rebels burned the Railroad bridge today' (entry description claim confirmed). Other entries: 'Saturday, June 27 ... The Rebels entered town at ten O clock this morning General Jenkins- Brigade of Calvary'; 'Wednesday, July 1 ... The Garrison bruned by the Rebels about 10,000 of our troops came up here from Harrisburg with three batteries ... the Rebels shelled the town'; 'Saturday, July 4 ... the citizens are fixing up the College for a Hospital'; 'Monday, July 6 ... two Gentlemen here ... are going to the Battlefield tomorrow'. Weekdays are consistent with 1863 (24 June 1863 was a Wednesday). Historical cross-checks in cached OR vol. 27 pt 2 OCR: Ewell's corps 'occupied [Carlisle] on the 27th'; 'Brigadier-General Smith advanced to Carlisle July 1, with 3,000 men ... Lee's cavalry ... shelled the town'; 'The enemy set fire to ... the barracks'; and a Union account of arriving at Carlisle 'saw the ruins of the barracks and the railroad bridge outside, destroyed by the rebels'. The PDF itself names no author, repository or transcriber (no header); 'CCHS' appears only in the file name, and 'transcribed by Frank Kline' and 'young girl' come from the House Divided blog post 'Beyond Gettysburg: Primary Sources for the Gettysburg Campaign' ('The unknown young girl wrote on Monday, June 29 that, "The Rebels are going in every house and stealing all they can"').
extraction_notes: Born-digital Word-to-PDF with a clean text layer (2 pages, ~4.1 KB). One passage per dated entry (15 passages), each already carrying its date; keep the author's spelling ('Getesburg', 'bruned') and the transcriber's brackets ('[4]') and braces. The writer is not identified (mentions Duff, Ed, Arch, Mother, Pappy, Sis, Willie), so attribute as 'anonymous young Carlisle resident'. Note 'the Garrison' = Carlisle Barracks.
issues: Anonymous: no author, no repository and no transcriber named in the PDF; 'CCHS' and 'Frank Kline' are only in the filename and the House Divided post (unverified against the CCHS original).
'Young girl' is the post's inference; the text is consistent with a young woman but does not state age or sex.
Transcription is the only text; not checked against the manuscript (no scan available).

Only second-hand rumors about the battle (e.g. July 5: 'we captured 118 cannon 25,000 prisoners'); no eyewitness battle description. Gettysburg relevance is the Carlisle occupation, shelling and aftermath.
Entry title omits that the diary runs 24 June to 8 July; an attributable date range is better than 'June-July 1863'.

written: Composed c.1866 (begun in Canada) to 1894; first published posthumously Nov. 1912 (J. B. Lippincott, copyright notice 1913); York/Wrightsville text expands his 22 Aug 1863 official report
rights_basis: Imprint year confirmed from the scanned title page ('Philadelphia & London, J. B. Lippincott Company, 1912'; 'Published November, 1912'; 'Copyright, 1913'); IA metadata date 1912; Google Books shows 'Full view'. US public domain by date (published before 1931). Editor's notes by R. H. Early (1912) are PD by the same date. DocSouth (UNC) TEI header carries rightsstatements.org 'No Copyright - United States 1.0' (the item is believed PD in the US; other countries not determined). DocSouth electronic edition 1999; its page header says site archived 3/30/26.
evidence: Link: the exact URL has dq= and pg= parameters that books.google.com/robots.txt disallows, so I did not fetch it. I fetched the bare https://books.google.com/books?id=0xtCAAAAIAAJ (HTTP 200): 'Lieutenant General Jubal Anderson Early, C.S.A.: Autobiographical Sketch and Narrative of the War Between the States', J.B. Lippincott 1912, 496 pages, 'Full view'. The contents list shows chapter XXIV at p.253. I then read the full text on archive.org (item lieutenantgeneraearl, UNC Chapel Hill scan, imagecount 560, ABBYY OCR) and the DocSouth TEI XML (docsouth.unc.edu/fpn/early/early.xml, 516 <pb> markers, chapter 'AT YORK AND WRIGHTSVILLE' at p.253). Description claims checked: (1) occupation of York. Early writes 'I then levied a contribution on the town for 100,000 dollars in money, 2,000 pairs of shoes, 1,000 hats, 1,000 pairs of socks, and three days' rations' and later that '$28,600 in money' was furnished; Hoke's brigade under Col. Avery was quartered in the hospital buildings; cars were burned but the car shops and depots spared (p.259-263). (2) Wrightsville bridge: Gordon 'found it on fire' half-way across, 'The bridge was entirely consumed', and Early 'regretted this very much' because it thwarted his plan to cross the Susquehanna (pp.259-261). Cross-check: the same facts, the $28,600 figure and Gordon entering York on the 28th appear in Early's 22 Aug 1863 report, OR 27 pt 2 No. 470, in the repo OR27 cache. Date of writing: the editor's note says the manuscript 'was left in manuscript form' at his death on 2 March 1894 and its 'preparation covered the term of years beginning immediately after the close of the war'. The editor's intro says it was at least commenced in Canada, with a related letter written in 1866.
extraction_notes: Best source is the DocSouth TEI XML or HTML (docsouth.unc.edu/fpn/early/early.xml / early.html): human-corrected text, <pb n=...> page markers placed at the start of each page, <head> chapter divisions (this chapter is labelled CHAPTER XXIII in the TEI, 'At York and Wrightsville' p.253 in the printed contents). The IA ABBYY OCR (lieutenantgeneraearl_djvu.txt) is a clean fallback but has no form feeds; its page numbers are at the page foot (e.g. '259' ends the page that begins 'event that it should be defended'), which is easy to mis-assign. Segment by paragraph with printed page; one footnote on p.262-263 reproduces Early's address 'To the Citizens of York'. Page map (DocSouth pb): p.257 = Gettysburg occupation 26 June (26th Pa Militia); p.259 = York entered 28 June, requisition, Gordon sent to Wrightsville; pp.260-261 = bridge burned; p.261-262 = amounts furnished; p.262-263 = cars burned, address to York citizens. The linked anchor (pg=PA257) lands on p.257, about two pages before the York occupation begins. Quote only after a verbatim check against DocSouth/IA.
issues: Exact Google Books URL (dq=, pg=PA257) not fetched: robots.txt disallows those parameters; only the bare id page was checked.

Page anchor is off by about 2 pages: printed p.257 is Early's 26 June occupation of Gettysburg and the 26th Pennsylvania Militia; York begins p.259 and the Wrightsville bridge pp.259-261. Chapter start is p.253.

Retrospective, partisan memoir: composed 1866-1894 and published 1912 by the editor (R. H. Early); the York/Wrightsville passage is an expansion of Early's official report of 22 Aug 1863 (OR 27 pt 2 No. 470), so it is not independent evidence. Early's statement that the militia fired the bridge ('inflammable materials having previously been prepared') is his own account.
Title 'memoir pages' is vague; do not confuse with Early's separate 1866/67 'A Memoir of the Last Year of the War for Independence' (1864-65 only).

Early's own account of the Wrightsville bridge and the number of shoes (1,200-1,500 furnished) differs slightly from the newspaper account in entry 593 ($28,000, 30,000 rations): minor, expected between sources.

written: Original published in the Baltimore Gazette (date not given), summer 1863; reprinted in the Raleigh Daily Progress on Fri 14 Aug 1863 (per the blog); blog post published 22 Oct 2015, modified 8 Oct 2020
rights_basis: The page footer reads '(c) 2026 York Daily Record/Sunday News' and no open licence is stated. The blog post (Scott Mingus, Cannonball) interleaves bracketed editorial notes and captions with the 1863 text, so the blog's presentation is copyrighted even though the 1863 newspaper text itself would be public domain. The original Baltimore Gazette or Raleigh Daily Progress page image was not located (two Chronicling America queries returned no match), so no public-domain source is in hand.
evidence: The URL returned 301 (http to https; the /2015/10/22/ date path was dropped) to https://yorkblog.com/cannonball/eyewitness-account-of-the-confederate-occupation-of-york-pa/ (HTTP 200, 61 KB, robots.txt allows crawling). The page title is 'New eyewitness account of the Confederate occupation of York, Pa. - Cannonball', posted by Scott Mingus on 22 Oct 2015 (Yoast: published 2015-10-23T02:13Z, modified 2020-10-08). The post says the story ran in The Daily Progress (Raleigh, N.C.) on Friday 14 Aug 1863, repeating an item from the Baltimore Gazette, and that it is an account written by an eyewitness in York of Early's three-day occupation. Description claims checked: (1) 'newspaper account / civilian': the quoted text uses first-person plural for York's townspeople ('our anxious citizens', 'our humiliating presence'), consistent with a York resident writer; the author is not named. (2) 'reprinted by the York Daily Record's Civil War blog': the footer credits York Daily Record/Sunday News and the blog is Cannonball. Content cross-checks against Early's memoir and report (entry 592): Gordon's brigade enters York Sunday 28 June around 10 a.m.; Early demands $100,000 and supplies, receives about $28,000; Avery's men in town, Hays' and Smith's brigades camped outside; Early spares the railroad car shops, burning only a few cars; the column leaves west on Tuesday 30 June.
extraction_notes: WordPress HTML article, not a page image. The quoted newspaper text is in running paragraphs interrupted by the blogger's bracketed editor's notes and image captions, so passages would have to be cut at brackets. Not suitable for the quote corpus because of the host's copyright. A 'Raleigh Daily Progress 14 Aug 1863' or 'Baltimore Gazette' page image from DigitalNC or Chronicling America would be the proper primary source; my two Chronicling America full-text queries found nothing.
issues: Author unidentified; the Baltimore Gazette original and its date are not given, so the item is a second-hand reprint of a reprint, with the blogger's transcription not checked against a page image.
Host copyright (York Daily Record); the quotable 1863 text must be re-sourced from the original newspaper.
URL as listed redirects (http to https, date path removed); use the canonical URL.
Transcription slip visible on the page: '$100,00' in the demand (should read $100,000).
'Contemporary civilian' status of the author is inferred from the text and the blogger's statement, not independently verified.

Dayton, 1896'); the OCR of the title page itself shows no year. Published before 1931, so US public domain. evidence: Link: the exact URL (dq=, pg=PA193) is disallowed for bots by robots.txt, so I did not fetch it. Extraction should cover chapters XVIII-XX (pp.192-229). written: Written 1865 (about two years after the events, 'with the aid of notes taken while the events were occurring'); found among the author's papers after his death in 1893; published posthumously 1899 (Richmond, B. F. Johnson), edited by his son G. W. Beale
rights_basis: Title page (OCR): 'Richmond, Va.: B. F. Johnson Publishing Company. 1899'. archive.org metadata (item historyofninthvi00beal): date 1899, 'possible-copyright-status: NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT', copyright-evidence 'no visible notice of copyright; stated date is 1899' (rebecca.m, 16 June 2008). Published before 1931, so US public domain. Chapter headings and the roster were added by the editor.
evidence: The URL https://archive.org/stream/historyofninthvi00beal#page/84/mode/2up returns 200 via redirect to /details/historyofninthvi00beal?view=theater. Metadata: 'History of the Ninth Virginia cavalry, in the war between the states', Beale, R. L. T. (Richard Lee Tuberville), 1819-1893, Richmond, B. F. Johnson, 1899, imagecount 208, NYPL scan. I read the full IA djvu text (412 KB) and the page map. Page-anchor check: IA page_numbers.json maps leaf 96 to printed p.84 (leaves 92-95 are unnumbered), and the djvu.xml page file historyofninthvi00beal_0096 is the page whose running head is 'History of the Ninth Virginia Cavalry' and begins 'Among them was a young surgeon', ending with Carlisle. So #page/84 lands exactly on the Carlisle shelling. Description claims checked: (1) Stuart's ride and Carlisle shelling: chapter VIII covers Rockville, Hanover (30 June) and, on p.84, 'Nightfall found us in the vicinity of Carlisle'; a demand to surrender was 'declined, and our cannons opened. The United States barracks blazed. The women screamed.' (2) author a Dickinson man: on p.84 he recalls 'when a student at Dickinson College' hunting over these grounds. 'Colonel' and 'Class of 1838': the book calls him 'Late Brig. General' and 'their old commander'; Dickinson's House Divided blog post 'The Lives of Richard and George Beale' (fetched, 200) states he graduated with the Class of 1838, served in the 9th Va. Cavalry 'until he became the leading colonel of the regiment', and quotes this same Carlisle passage; Wikipedia (raw wikitext, fetched) gives colonel from 15 Sept 1862. These are secondary and not the college's own record. The Introductory Note says the narrative 'was written ... in 1865', was found 'among his papers at his death, on April 17, 1893, written upon the consecutive pages of a thin blank-book', and 'carefully copied, and arranged in chapters with headings'. Cross-check with entry 597: G. W. Beale's July 1863 letter names Captain Billingsley of the regiment captured at Hanover, matching this book's loss of 'Captain Billingsley' there.
extraction_notes: ABBYY OCR (historyofninthvi00beal_djvu.txt, 412 KB; also _djvu.xml with word coordinates) with moderate errors: 'Dickinson' as 'Dickinson', 'hunted' as 'himted', 'surrender' as 'siu^render', header 'History of the Ninth Virginia Cavalry' as 'Nintli' or 'NinfJi'; printed page numbers in the OCR running heads are unreliable ('8 /J.' for 84, '8j' for 83/85), so map pages with IA's page_numbers.json (202 numbered leaves of 208 images; leaf n = leaf+0 as printed in that file) and use the djvu.xml page files to confirm. Structure: 192 pages of narrative in about 12 chapters headed by the editor, then roster and incomplete casualty list. Segment by chapter and paragraph; the Gettysburg material spans the second half of chapter VIII and chapter IX 'Retreat from Gettysburg' (p.~85-100). Quotes need a verbatim check against the OCR.
issues: Retrospective: written 1865 from notes (about 2 years after) and published 1899, so not contemporaneous; reflects the author's recollection and some hindsight.
The editor (G. W. B., his son) 'carefully copied' the manuscript and added chapter headings and the roster, so chapter titles and page-level structure are the editor's, not the author's.

'Class of 1838' and 'colonel at the time' are not stated in the book; they rest on the House Divided blog and Wikipedia (secondary). Beale's death date appears as 17 April 1893 in the book's note, 18 April in the blog and 21 April in Wikipedia: minor discrepancy, no effect on the entry.
archive.org/stream/ URL is redirected to the details page; the #page/84 fragment still resolves to printed p.84 in BookReader.
IA OCR is 'abbyy-to-hocr' with some low-confidence leaves (page_number_confidence 54), so page mapping near plates (leaves 92-95) should be checked on the images.

written: 13 July 1863 (letter to his mother, four miles northwest of Williamsport, Md.); published in SHSP vol. 11 (Jan-Dec 1883), pp.320-327
rights_basis: Text is a private letter of 1863 printed in SHSP vol. 11 whose own contents page reads 'January to December, 1883'; public domain by date. The IA metadata date field says 1876 (series start for every volume) and was not used. The linked gdg.org (Gettysburg Discussion Group) page is an unlicensed third-party transcription (last modified 2010) with a few textual differences, so the A1 tier applies to the SHSP text as read from the archive.org scan, not to the gdg copy.
evidence: The link returns 200 (19,702 bytes, HTML, Last-Modified 4 Sep 2010; the host has no robots.txt, 404). Heading on the page: 'A Soldier's Account of the Gettysburg Campaign. Letter from George W. Beale (son of General R. L. T. Beale)', dated July 13th, 1863, ending 'Source: Southern Historical Society Papers, Vol. 11, p.320-327'. I checked this against the SHSP scan: archive.org item southernhistoricv11sout (djvu text 1.7 MB). Its contents list 'Gettysburg Campaign - A Soldier's Letter, by George W. Beale 320'; the article starts on p.320 with the same heading and date and ends with 'G. W. Beale.' just before the next article (p.327-328), which matches pp.320-327; IA page_numbers.json maps leaf 332 to printed p.320 and leaf 339 to p.327. A word-multiset comparison of the gdg text with the SHSP OCR: about 3,430 vs 3,470 words with a handful of real differences (gdg has 'withing', 'Devine', 'until' where SHSP has 'till', and 'endeavored' where SHSP has 'endeavoured'), so the transcription is close but not verbatim. Description claims checked: (1) 'Confederate cavalryman': the author is a lieutenant leading a squadron of his regiment ('the squadron I commanded led'; company 'C' and 'K'); the regiment is identified as the 9th Virginia by 'Thirteenth and Ninth Virginia, and Second North Carolina' at Hanover and 'Captain Billingsly of this regiment' captured, matching entry 596's book; the Wikipedia/House Divided pages name him as a lieutenant in Co. C, 9th Va. Cav., son of Col. R. L. T. Beale. (2) 'Stuart's movements': the letter follows the ride from Salem through Fairfax, Rockville, Westminster and Hanover (30 June), where 'General Stuart sent an order for its [Carlisle's] surrender, which was refused' and he 'opened a terrible cannonade'; then Gettysburg on 2-3 July (the cavalry fight on the left with the Thirteenth and Ninth Virginia) and the pursuit to Hagerstown.
extraction_notes: Do not ingest from gdg.org. Use the SHSP vol. 11 scan on archive.org (southernhistoricv11sout; printed p.320 = leaf n332, p.327 = n339 per page_numbers.json) or any other page-image-backed copy, and do a verbatim check. SHSP is two-column running text with running heads ('320 Southern Historical Society Papers') that must be stripped; the letter is about 3,450 words, about 15 paragraphs, with a very short article heading, so it segments by paragraph with page numbers 320-327. The month/day of the first move is left blank in the original ('Thursday morning, June --'). The letter includes period racial terms for enslaved and free Black people; tag for sensitive-language handling in the Historian.
issues: The linked page is a third-party transcription, not the SHSP scan; it differs from the printed text in a few places ('withing', 'Devine', 'until' for 'till', 'endeavored', a doubled 'many of the'), and its <title> is empty.
The article is entitled 'A Soldier's Account of the Gettysburg Campaign' in the body but is listed as 'Gettysburg Campaign - A Soldier's Letter' in the volume contents: same item.

The entry title says '9th Virginia Cavalry', which the letter itself does not state outright; it is established from the Hanover paragraph and from entry 596 (father's regiment) and the House Divided blog.
IA metadata 'date' for the SHSP volume is 1876 (the series start), not 1883: use the volume's own contents/running heads for dating.
Written to his mother in the field in heavy rain, so it is a contemporaneous but unpolished and somewhat hearsay-laden account (e.g. losses and the Hagerstown fight reported second-hand).
